Fracture Mechanics 101

A crack concentrates stress and releases stored energy when it grows. Material joining its faces can resist that growth, and a metal that hardens changes the field at the tip. This page connects these physical pictures to the quantities used in MechanicsHarness cases. Read the explanation, use the formula, and check a small calculation before returning to your case.

How to use this page. Choose the term that stopped you. Check the conventions first if a length, sign or factor of two is unclear. The working is folded away so you can try each calculation yourself. All examples use hypothetical inputs, not measured material data.

0 Which length and which opening?

A centre crack has two ends, and both may advance. The original end is called the root; the advancing end is the current tip. Connectors are material connections that join the faces behind the tip. The opening is the distance between the faces, not the movement of one face.

In this growth picture, a is the original half-length, c is the current half-length, and L is the growth at each end.

In topics 8 and 9, a is the half-length of the open part and c is the half-length including the strips or bridged zones. These are the same letters as in the figure.

The coordinate x runs from the crack centre. The right root is at x = a, and the right tip is at x = c. The left side is their mirror image.

E′ is the effective elastic modulus. Here E is Young's modulus and ν is Poisson's ratio. Choose the branch matching the case's plane condition.

  • δ is the full face-to-face gap. For symmetric opening, it is twice either face's displacement from the symmetry plane.
  • Traction is force per unit area on a surface. Face pressure p > 0 opens the crack. A closing traction pulls the faces together and is represented by negative pressure.
  • G is the energy released, and Γ is the general symbol for the energy the material needs. Both are per unit crack-plane area. Count one crack area, not a separate area for each face.
  • Γ0 is the intrinsic toughness: the energy needed to separate material at the tip itself. Γb is the work absorbed by the connectors. Topics 7 and 9 explain the distinction.
  • Use Pa, m and J/m² in calculations. Stress intensity K, introduced next, is often reported in MPa √m. One MPa is 106 Pa. The symbol π is the circle constant.

Watch out. Growth of 5 mm at each end increases the total crack length by 10 mm, not 5 mm.

Try it. The original half-length is 20 mm and the current half-length is 25 mm. How far has each end grown? Use the growth-length formula. L = mm

Show the working

Both inputs are half-lengths, so no factor of two is needed in the subtraction:

Each end has grown 5.000 mm, so the total crack length has increased by 10 mm.

Used in: every case.

1 In which ways can a crack be loaded?

The two faces of a crack can move relative to each other in three basic ways, called modes. Any loading of a crack is a combination of them.

Mode I is opening: the faces move apart, normal to the crack plane. Mode II is in-plane sliding: the faces slide over each other, in the direction in which the crack points. Mode III is tearing: the faces slide past each other along the crack front, as when you tear a sheet of paper. Mode III is also called antiplane shear, because the only displacement is out of the plane of the picture.

Each mode has its own stress intensity factor, KI, KII and KIII, and each gives a stress that rises as the inverse square root of the distance to the tip (topic 3). For a straight crack that grows in its own plane, their energies add:

Here G is the energy release rate of topic 4, E′ is the effective modulus from Conventions, and μ is the shear modulus.

Most cases on this site are mode I, and on this page K without a subscript means KI. Antiplane shear appears in extra exercises because its mathematics is the simplest: there is one displacement, one equation, and often a closed-form answer.

Watch out. The mode describes the motion of the faces near the tip, not the load far away. A crack inclined to a tensile load is in mode I and mode II at once.

Try it. A crack carries KI = 3 MPa √m and KII = 4 MPa √m, with KIII = 0 and E′ = 100 GPa. Find the energy release rate. G = J/m²

Show the working

The two modes together release 250 J/m². Mode II supplies 160 of it, more than mode I, because the energy goes with the square of each intensity.

Used in: the HRR field, the extra exercise in antiplane shear.

2 Plane strain or plane stress?

Crack problems are usually solved in two dimensions, in the plane normal to the crack front. What happens in the third direction, along the front, then has to be assumed. There are two standard choices.

Plane strain is the model for a thick body. Away from its free surfaces, material near the crack front can hardly contract or expand along the front, because the material beside it holds it. The model sets the strain in that direction to zero, and a stress σzz builds up to keep it zero. Plane stress is the model for a thin sheet. Its two free surfaces carry no stress and are close together, so the model sets the stress through the thickness to zero, and the sheet is free to thin. Both are idealizations of a real plate.

Here z is the direction along the crack front, E is Young’s modulus, ν is Poisson’s ratio and μ is the shear modulus. The effective modulus E′ is the one used throughout this page. These relations are for a linear elastic solid.

For the same applied tractions, the two choices give the same in-plane stresses in a linear elastic body, and the same K. They differ in the strains, the opening and the energy release rate, all of which contain E′. Plane strain is the stiffer of the two.

The choice matters more once the material yields. The extra stress σzz of plane strain makes yielding harder, so the stresses near the tip are higher and the yielded region is smaller (topic 10).

Watch out. Plane strain does not mean that the out-of-plane stress is zero. It is the strain that is zero, and the stress is what keeps it so.

Try it. A steel has E = 200 GPa and ν = 0.3. Find its effective modulus in plane strain. E′ = GPa

Show the working

The plane-strain body is about 10 percent stiffer than the thin sheet, whose effective modulus is 200 GPa. For the same K, it opens less and releases less energy.

Used in: the HRR field, the problem, the poroelastic crack, the problem.

3 How strong is the stress concentration?

Pull a cracked plate and stress rises sharply near each tip. The stress intensity factor measures the strength of this near-tip stress field. At the same distance from the tip, a larger K means a larger stress. Opening the faces apart is called mode I.

The elastic model predicts a singularity: the stress grows without bound as the distance to the tip approaches zero. Real material instead yields or breaks in a small region called the separation zone.

KI is the mode-I stress intensity. Here Σ is the remote tensile stress, a is the crack half-length, and Y is a dimensionless geometry factor.

For a centre crack in a large plate, Y = 1. Other geometries need their own factor. Below, K means KI.

σyy is the tensile stress normal to the crack directly ahead of its tip. The distance from the tip is r.

Use this stress formula at distances larger than the separation zone but much smaller than the crack length. Such a region exists only if the separation zone is small compared with the crack.

Watch out. K is not a stress. Its units include a square root of length. The infinite elastic tip stress is not a physical material strength.

Try it. A large plate has a centre crack with half-length 10 mm under remote tension of 100 MPa. Use Y = 1 to find its intensity with the geometry formula. K = MPa √m

Show the working

Convert the half-length to metres, then evaluate the square-root factor:

The value 17.72 MPa √m sets the strength of the near-tip stress field; it is not the stress at the tip or a material strength.

Used in: crack bridging, steps 1 and 3.

4 Is there enough energy to grow?

When a crack advances, the body becomes more compliant. Stored elastic energy can be released, and the loading system may supply work as the body deforms. The energy available for each increment of crack area is G.

For a linear elastic mode-I crack, calculating this energy change gives:

G is the energy release rate, and E′ is the effective modulus from Conventions. The available energy scales with the square of the stress-field strength K and inversely with the stiffness E′.

Here “rate” means energy per increment of crack area, not per second. Energy toughness Γ has units J/m². K-toughness is the critical stress intensity for growth, usually reported in MPa √m. Substituting that critical intensity into the energy formula converts it to energy toughness.

Quasistatic growth is slow enough that inertia can be neglected. The crack stays put while G < Γ and can advance with G = Γ. Arrest means that the crack stops growing. If G > Γ, this criterion does not allow it to stop.

A quasistatic calculation follows successive states, not motion through time.

Watch out. Equality balances available and required energy. It does not say whether a small advance will settle or run away. That stability question is discussed in topic 9.

Try it. Take K = 2 MPa √m and E′ = 100 GPa. Compute the energy release rate with the formula above, then compare it with Γ = 50 J/m². G = J/m²

Show the working

Convert to Pa-based units before squaring the intensity:

The available energy is 40.00 J/m², below the required 50 J/m², so the crack stays put under the stated criterion.

Used in: crack bridging, steps 1 and 2.

5 How do face loads change the tip field?

Linear elasticity lets us add solutions. A plate under remote tension with unloaded crack faces can be represented by an uncracked stretched plate plus a pressure-loaded crack. The pressure-loaded crack is an auxiliary problem: a simpler helper problem used to construct the real solution.

The auxiliary pressure cancels the forces that the uncracked solution carries across the future crack plane, leaving the combined faces unloaded. The uncracked solution has no singular stress field or face-to-face gap, so the auxiliary problem supplies all of K and the opening.

K is the right-tip intensity, c is the current half-length, x is the position from the centre, and p(x) is the symmetric face pressure.

This pressure solution is for a large plate with no remote load. The integral gives more weight to pressure near the tip. Thus, K depends on where the traction acts, not only on the total force.

Σ is the uniform opening pressure. The positive quantity σb is the magnitude of the closing traction exerted by connectors on a < |x| < c. The roots are at ±a, and the tips are at ±c.

To represent remote tension, use a uniform auxiliary face pressure equal to the remote tensile stress Σ. The second term subtracts the connectors' effect. This reduction of the tip intensity is called shielding. Evaluate arccos in radians.

Watch out. A positive connector strength represents a closing load, so its face pressure is negative. Adding its magnitude would increase the tip intensity.

Try it. Use c = 10 mm, a = 5 mm, Σ = 20 MPa and σb = 15 MPa. Find the net intensity with the second formula above. K = MPa √m

Show the working

Convert the lengths to 0.01000 m and 0.005000 m. Their ratio is 0.5, whose inverse cosine is π/3 radians. Evaluate the driving and shielding terms separately:

The connectors reduce the intensity from about 3.545 to 1.772 MPa √m, halving the strength of the near-tip field in this example.

Where this comes from

The uniform-pressure integral gives the first term. For the closing strips, the factor before the pressure integral already accounts for symmetry. The remaining interval integral is:

The antiderivative follows by substituting x = c sin θ. Multiplying this integral by the factor before the integral and by the negative strip pressure gives the shielding term.

Used in: crack bridging, step 3.

6 What shape does an open crack take?

Uniform pressure pushes the upper face up and the lower face down. For a centre crack in a large elastic plate, the opening is elliptical. It is widest at the centre and zero at both tips.

δ(x) is the full gap at position x. Here p is the uniform positive face pressure, c is the crack half-length, and E′ is the effective modulus.

Use positions between the tips. Doubling the pressure doubles the opening; doubling the modulus halves it.

For remote tension with unloaded crack faces, topic 5 replaces the remote stress by an equal auxiliary face pressure. Use that pressure in this formula to obtain the same opening.

Watch out. Do not double this result: it is already the full gap. One face's displacement from the symmetry plane is half of it.

Try it. Take p = 10 MPa, E′ = 100 GPa and c = 10 mm. Find the full gap at x = 6 mm with the elliptical-opening formula. δ = µm

Show the working

Use metres and Pa throughout the substitution:

The full gap is 3.200 µm, so each face moves 1.600 µm from the symmetry plane.

Used in: crack bridging, step 4, the poroelastic crack, step 1.

7 How much work do connectors absorb?

Connectors resist separation of the faces. A traction-gap law gives their resisting traction as the gap increases. The area under this curve is the work absorbed per unit crack-plane area, not a physical surface area. Constant traction gives a rectangular area up to the failure gap.

Γb is the connector work per unit crack-plane area. The function t(δ) gives the resisting traction magnitude at full gap δ. The failure gap is δc, and σb is the constant traction magnitude.

This is called a cohesive or bridging law: it describes how connections between the faces resist opening. Its work uses the positive resisting magnitude, although its equivalent face pressure is negative. Using the full gap already includes the work of both faces.

The wake is the region behind the advancing tip, where connectors absorb work. The tip only feels the stress field around it, whose intensity already includes the connectors' shielding; the connectors act behind it, so their work is accounted for separately.

The local tip growth condition therefore uses intrinsic toughness Γ0 alone. Do not put Γ0 + σbδc into that local condition. Topic 9 explains when their sum can represent the resistance of the whole crack.

Watch out. The area under the law is energy per unit area, not force. Do not multiply it by two for the two faces.

Try it. A constant traction of 20 MPa acts until the full gap reaches 50 µm. Compute the work per unit crack-plane area using the constant-traction product. Γb = J/m²

Show the working

Convert the traction to Pa and the failure gap to metres. The rectangle's area is their product:

The connectors absorb 1,000 J for each square metre of crack-plane area opened to their failure gap, with no extra factor for the two faces.

Used in: crack bridging, steps 1 and 2.

8 Can a crack open with zero tip intensity?

In Dugdale's strip-yield model, the strips represent a thin yielded zone where material has deformed permanently; here, they represent any zone that pulls the faces together with a constant traction. The central slit has no traction on its faces, and the resisting strips extend from its ends to the outer tips.

The remote stress and the closing tractions act together. At a particular load, their singular parts cancel at x = c, making K zero there. The opening is the net effect of both loads.

ΣD is the remote tensile stress giving zero outer-tip intensity. Here σb is the closing-traction magnitude, a is the half-length of the open part, and c is the half-length including the strips.

This load follows from topic 5's net-intensity formula by setting K = 0.

δ(a) is the full gap at the right root, and E′ is the effective modulus. The symbol ln means the natural logarithm.

The gap formula adds the openings produced by the remote stress and the closing tractions at this load. Zero K removes only the singular stress term at the outer tip; it does not remove the finite deformation produced throughout the body, so the central crack can remain open.

This constant-traction solution can describe either yielded strips or other closing connections. A tip that requires nonzero intrinsic toughness needs an additional tip field; this zero-K solution alone is not sufficient.

Watch out. The outer tip at x = c and the root at x = a are different places.

Try it. Set the remote load to ΣD. With a = 10 mm, c = 20 mm, σb = 30 MPa and E′ = 100 GPa, find the root gap with the gap formula above. δ(a) = µm

Show the working

The length ratio is 2, with natural logarithm 0.6931472. Substitute in Pa and m, and check the remote load separately:

At a remote stress of 20 MPa, the root gap is 5.295 µm even though the singular stress intensity at the outer tips is zero.

Used in: crack bridging, step 4 and the find-the-error tests.

9 When can bridging become a toughness?

The bridged zone is the region behind the tip where connectors still join the faces. Small-scale bridging means that this zone is much shorter than the crack and the relevant body dimensions. In that limit, its total work can represent its contribution to toughness.

For a long zone, solve the elastic body equations and the connector law together. The body equations give the gap under the applied load and connector tractions. The law gives the traction at that gap, so both must agree.

ℓ is a material length scale. Here E′ is the effective modulus, δc is the connector failure gap, and σb is the constant resisting-traction magnitude.

ℓ is not the actual zone length. That length depends on loading, geometry and the traction law. The ratio Γ0 / (σbδc) also affects the solution; it does not by itself establish small-scale bridging.

Γ is the effective energy toughness, Γ0 is the intrinsic tip toughness, and Γb is the connector work per unit crack-plane area. This sum describes the resistance of the whole crack in the small-scale limit, not the local tip condition in topic 7.

This page cannot give a numerical threshold for “small-scale.” Compare the computed zone length, c − a at each end, with the crack length and the body dimensions, such as plate width and distances to nearby boundaries. The case studies do exactly that. For large-scale bridging, where the zone is not small by these comparisons, use both the body solution and the traction law.

Under load control, a small advance is stable if further growth requires a higher load. If further growth requires a lower load, the applied load can drive continued growth. The maximum marks the loss of this stability. Displacement control can behave differently, so identify what the loading system controls.

Watch out. A material length is not a computed zone size. An energy balance is not a stability guarantee.

Try it. Take E′ = 100 GPa, δc = 20 µm and σb = 100 MPa. Compute the material length with its formula above, without treating it as the zone length. ℓ = mm

Show the working

Use SI units for the substitution, then convert to millimetres:

The value 20.00 mm is a material length scale, not a prediction of the bridged zone length or proof that bridging is small-scale.

Used in: crack bridging, step 1 and the explorer.

10 How large is the yielded region?

The elastic field of topic 3 predicts a stress that rises without limit at the tip. A metal cannot carry that: close to the tip it yields, which means that it deforms permanently. The yielded region is called the plastic zone.

A first estimate of its size asks where the elastic stress ahead of the tip equals the yield stress:

Here rp is the estimated size of the plastic zone ahead of the tip, K is the stress intensity factor and σY is the yield stress in a tension test. The first form is for plane stress. In plane strain (topic 2) the stress along the crack front makes yielding harder, and the usual estimate is three times smaller. These are first estimates of the scale, due to Irwin, not exact sizes. Inside the zone the stress is redistributed, and a metal that hardens carries more than its yield stress there (topic 13).

Small-scale yielding means that the plastic zone is much smaller than the crack length, the uncracked width ahead of the crack, and the other in-plane dimensions of the body. The elastic field with its K then still holds in a ring around the zone. For a given material, K is the only thing the zone feels of the loading and of the shape of the body. In that case the J integral can be taken from the elastic field, J = K²/E′ (topic 11).

If the plastic zone is not small, there is no such ring, and K no longer describes the field near the tip. J may still do so, under the conditions of topics 11 and 12, but it then has to be computed from an analysis of the whole yielding body.

Watch out. Small-scale yielding is a comparison of two lengths, not a property of the material. The same steel can be in small-scale yielding in a large plate and far from it in a small specimen.

Try it. A plate has K = 30 MPa √m and σY = 400 MPa. Estimate the plastic zone size in plane stress. rp = mm

Show the working

The zone is a little under one millimetre. For a crack of 10 mm half-length the zone is about 9 percent of that length. Whether this counts as small-scale yielding also depends on the other dimensions of the plate. In plane strain the estimate would be a third of this, about 0.3 mm.

Used in: the HRR field, the checks and limits of step 4.

11 How much energy flows to the tip?

Draw any curve around the crack tip. Start on the lower face, go anticlockwise, and end on the upper face. Across this curve, the material outside does work on the material inside, and the material inside stores energy. The J integral adds these contributions along the curve. Its value is the energy that reaches the tip per unit crack advance, per unit thickness of the body.

Here Γ is the curve and ds is a short length along it. W is the strain energy density, the stored work per unit volume. N is the unit normal to the curve that points outward, away from the tip, and Nx is its x component. The traction ti is the force per unit area that the outside material exerts on the inside, and ui is the displacement. A repeated index means a sum over the directions.

The units of J are stress times length, N/m, which is the same as J/m². Rice introduced this integral in 1968.

Path independence means that every such curve gives the same value. For a crack that is not growing, loaded slowly and at small strains, it holds when four conditions are met. The material is elastic, linear or nonlinear, so that the stress follows from one energy density W. There are no body forces, which are forces acting throughout the volume, such as weight. The crack faces are straight and free of traction. The material properties do not change along x.

Path independence is what makes J useful. You can evaluate it on a far curve, where the field is known, and then use the same value on a tiny circle at the tip, where the field is wanted.

For a linear elastic body in mode I, J equals the energy release rate of topic 4:

Here G is the energy release rate, K is the stress intensity factor and E′ is the effective modulus from Conventions.

A metal that deforms plastically keeps some strain after it is unloaded, so it is not elastic. But while the loading only increases, with the stress components growing in proportion to each other, it follows one stress-strain curve, much as a nonlinear elastic material would (topic 12). J is path independent for that nonlinear elastic model, and this is the sense in which it is used for metals. Once part of the body unloads, for example behind a growing crack, path independence is lost.

Watch out. J measures the energy flow to the tip. Whether the crack grows needs a material criterion in addition. When you evaluate J, keep every term: the traction term has one part for each traction component.

Try it. A linear elastic body has K = 30 MPa √m and E′ = 200 GPa. Find J with the formula above. J = kJ/m²

Show the working

Convert to Pa-based units before squaring the intensity:

The tip receives 4.5 kJ for each square metre of new crack area. Whether that is enough for growth depends on the material.

Used in: the HRR field, steps 1 and 3.

12 What does a hardening material do?

Pull a metal bar past its yield point, where permanent strain begins. The bar keeps carrying more stress as it stretches, but each further bit of strain needs less extra stress than in the elastic range. This is hardening.

A simple model for a bar under stress in one direction is a power law:

Here ε is the strain and σ is the stress. The reference stress σ0 and the reference strain ε0 set the scales, E is Young’s modulus, α is a dimensionless coefficient, and n is the hardening exponent.

For n = 1 the material is linear. For a large n the curve becomes nearly flat: once the stress is near σ0, a small increase in stress gives a large increase in strain. So in this convention a larger n means less hardening. Some books use the inverse exponent N = 1/n instead.

The energy density W is the area under the stress-strain curve:

For n = 1 this is the familiar one half of stress times strain.

A crack tip has several stress components at once. Plastic strain in a metal responds to shear, which changes shape, and not to pressure, which changes volume. So first remove the mean normal stress. What remains is the stress deviator, and its size is measured by the effective stress, also called the von Mises stress:

Here sij is the deviator of the stress σij, and σkk is the sum of the three normal stresses. The symbol δij is one when the two indices are equal and zero otherwise. A repeated index means a sum. In a tension test, σe equals the tensile stress. The power law for all components is then:

The strain εij has the direction of the deviator, and its size follows the power law of the bar. There is no volume change.

This law gives the total strain directly from the current stress, so it is a nonlinear elastic law. It describes a real metal only while the loading keeps increasing, with the stress components growing in proportion and no unloading. That is the condition under which the path-independent J of topic 11 applies.

Watch out. The pure power law has no separate elastic part and no yield point. It is meant for the region where plastic strain dominates. Also check which exponent convention a source uses, n or 1/n.

Try it. Take σ0 = 400 MPa, ε0 = 0.002, α = 1 and n = 5. Find the strain at a stress of 600 MPa with the power law. ε = %

Show the working

The stress is only 1.5 times the reference stress, but the strain is about 7.6 times the reference strain, 1.519 percent. In this model the energy density is 7.594 MJ/m³. In a real metal most of that work is not recoverable.

Used in: the HRR field, the problem and step 1.

13 What is the field near a crack in a hardening material?

In topic 3, the elastic stress rises as the inverse square root of the distance to the tip, and so does the strain. In a hardening material the rise is divided differently: the stress rises more slowly, and the strain rises faster.

The reason comes from J (topic 11). Evaluate it on a circle of radius r around the tip. The length of the circle is proportional to r, and J is the same on every circle. Suppose the field keeps the same shape around the tip at every distance. Then every term of J varies with distance as the energy density does, and the energy density must vary as 1/r. In the power-law material the strain varies as the stress to the power n, so:

The symbol ∼ means “varies as, with constants left out”. For n = 1 both powers are one half, which is the elastic field.

The leading field near the tip is:

Here σ0, ε0, α and n are the constants of the power law in topic 12. The polar coordinates r and θ are centred at the tip, with θ = 0 directly ahead. The functions σ̃ij(θ) are dimensionless and give the shape of the field around the tip. They are scaled so that the largest effective stress over all angles is one. In is a dimensionless number that comes from putting this field into the J integral.

This is called the HRR field, after Hutchinson, and Rice and Rosengren, who found it in 1968. In it, J sets the amplitude of the near-tip field, as K does in an elastic body. Two bodies of the same material with the same J, both in plane strain or both in plane stress, have the same near-tip field wherever this field dominates.

The angular functions and In depend on n and on whether the body is in plane strain or plane stress. Except for n = 1, they must be computed numerically. For the opening mode in plane strain, the reference calculation of the HRR case study gives:

Hardening exponent nIn
16.283
35.507
6.54.818
134.401

The field holds very close to the tip compared with the size of the plastic zone, the region where plastic strain is important. It does not hold in the tiny region at the tip itself, where the strains are large and the tip has blunted, meaning that deformation has rounded it. It assumes small strain and no unloading.

Watch out. The infinite stress and strain at r = 0 belong to the model, not to the material. The exponent of the stress is 1/(n + 1), not 1/n.

Try it. Take n = 4. By what factor does the stress rise when the distance to the tip falls by a factor of 32? factor =

Show the working

The stress varies as the distance to the power −1/5:

The stress only doubles. In an elastic body it would rise by a factor of 5.657. The strain takes most of the rise: it grows by a factor of 16.

Used in: the HRR field, steps 2 to 4.

14 What changes when the pores are full of fluid?

Rock, soil, gels and many tissues are solids with small connected spaces, called pores, that are filled with fluid. Squeeze a wet sponge quickly and it feels stiff: the water has no time to escape, so it carries part of the load. Squeeze it slowly and it feels softer: the water leaves, and the solid framework carries the load alone.

A poroelastic solid is the model for this. It has two fields: the stress in the solid as a whole, and the pore pressure p of the fluid. Each affects the other. Compressing the solid raises the pore pressure, and a pore pressure pushes the framework apart.

Two limits are ordinary elasticity. The response is undrained when the load changes so fast that every bit of material keeps its fluid. It is drained when the fluid has had time to flow and the pore pressure has returned to its surrounding value. Fluid carries no shear, so both limits have the same shear modulus. This page writes the shear modulus as μ; the poroelastic case writes it as G. The two limits differ in Poisson’s ratio: ν when drained, and a larger value νu when undrained. In plane strain the effective modulus of Conventions is therefore:

The undrained solid is the stiffer one. Every elastic formula on this page holds in each limit, with the Poisson ratio of that limit.

How much pore pressure does a sudden load create? In plane strain, before any fluid has moved:

Here σxx + σyy is the sum of the two in-plane normal stresses, with tension positive, so compression gives a positive pressure. Stresses and pressure are changes from the state before loading. The Biot coefficient α, between 0 and 1, measures how strongly the pore pressure acts on the solid framework.

Watch out. A pressure applied to a surface and the pore pressure inside the solid are different quantities. A crack face can carry an applied pressure while the pore pressure on it is held at zero. Also, “undrained” and “drained” describe how fast the load is compared with the flow, not two different materials.

Try it. A solid has ν = 0.25, νu = 0.35 and α = 0.8. It is suddenly compressed in plane strain with σxx = σyy = −10 MPa. Find the pore pressure before any fluid moves. p = MPa

Show the working

The pore pressure rises by 5 MPa, half of the applied compression. That pressure then drives the fluid towards any place where the pressure is lower.

Used in: the poroelastic crack, steps 1 and 2.

15 How far does the fluid get in a given time?

Fluid flows from high pore pressure to low, and faster where the pressure changes more steeply. This is Darcy’s law. Together with the fact that fluid is not created or lost, it makes a pressure difference spread out and fade in the way heat does. The process is called diffusion.

The simplest example has flow in one direction only. A uniform solid fills the region on one side of a flat face. Its pore pressure has suddenly been raised to p0, and the pressure on the face is held at zero. The pressure at a distance y from the face, after a time t, is:

Here erf is the error function, which rises from 0 to 1, and c is the diffusivity, in units of length squared per time. A more permeable or stiffer solid has a larger c.

Time and distance appear only in the combination y/⁠√(ct). So the curve keeps its shape and simply stretches as time passes. The length that sets its width is the diffusion length:

The second form gives the time after which the change has reached a distance ℓ. It grows as the square of the distance: reaching ten times farther takes a hundred times longer. At the distance √(ct) itself the pressure has fallen only about halfway, as the dots in the figure show.

This has a consequence that is easy to miss. Whether a time is “short” depends on where you look. At a point much farther than √(ct) from a drained boundary, the solid is still nearly undrained. At a point much closer than √(ct), it is already nearly drained. Both are true at the same moment.

Watch out. The diffusion length is a scale, not a sharp boundary: the figure shows a smooth change. And a short time for a large body is not a short time for a small region inside it.

Try it. A rock has diffusivity c = 1 mm²/s. How far has the pressure change spread after 100 s? ⁠√(ct) = mm

Show the working

After 100 s the layer affected by drainage is about 10 mm thick. To reach 100 mm would take 10 000 s, a hundred times longer.

Used in: the poroelastic crack, the picture and step 3.

16 What does a material with memory do?

A polymer or a gel is stiff when it is loaded quickly and softer when it is loaded slowly. Under a constant load it keeps deforming, which is called creep. Its strain depends on how it was loaded in the past, not only on the present stress: it remembers its loading history. Such a material is viscoelastic.

The simplest model with both behaviours is the standard linear solid, the model of the viscoelastic crack study. It is written here for shear, because that study is in antiplane shear (topic 1). A spring of shear modulus G∞ acts in parallel with a branch in which a spring of modulus G0 − G∞ is in series with a dashpot. A dashpot is a piston in a viscous fluid; it resists the rate of deformation.

Loaded suddenly, the dashpot has no time to move, so both springs carry the load, and the solid responds with the instantaneous modulus G∞ + (G0 − G∞) = G0. Held for a long time, the dashpot flows until its branch carries no stress, and the solid responds with the long-term modulus G∞. Their ratio λ = G∞/G0 is less than one. A small λ means a strongly viscoelastic solid. Here a G with a subscript is a shear modulus, written μ elsewhere on this page, not the energy release rate of topic 4.

The creep compliance C(t) is the strain per unit stress, for a stress applied suddenly at t = 0 and then held:

Here tc is the creep time, the time scale on which C grows from C(0) = 1/G0 to C(∞) = 1/G∞. Hui and Long (2026, Eqs. 5 to 7) use the same function.

Any loading history is a sequence of small increments of stress. In a linear material each increment keeps producing strain according to C, counted from when it was applied, and the strains add. This is Boltzmann superposition:

Here γ is the shear strain, τ is the shear stress, and s is the time at which an increment was applied. This is what “memory” means: an old increment still contributes, with the weight C(t − s). A stress τ applied suddenly at t = 0 and held gives γ = τC(t).

Watch out. The creep time tc, over which the strain grows under a fixed stress, is not the relaxation time, over which the stress falls under a fixed strain. For the standard linear solid the relaxation time is λtc, shorter by the factor λ. Check which of the two a source quotes.

Try it. A standard linear solid has G∞ = 1 MPa, G0 = 10 MPa and tc = 2 s. A shear stress of 0.1 MPa is applied suddenly and held. Find the shear strain at t = tc. γ =

Show the working

The strain jumps at once to 0.01, the response with the instantaneous modulus. By t = tc it has grown to 0.0669, and it creeps on towards 0.1, ten times its first value.

Used in: the viscoelastic crack, the problem and steps 1 to 4.

17 Why does a faster crack need more energy?

Peeling tape off quickly takes more force than peeling it slowly. In a viscoelastic solid, part of the energy that a crack releases is lost in the bulk material around it, and how much is lost depends on the speed of the crack.

The crack runs at a constant speed v, with a cohesive zone of length lc ahead of its tip, a strip zone as in topic 8. In antiplane shear the zone carries a constant shear stress τc and breaks when the sliding across it, the full jump in displacement, reaches δc. Its work per unit crack advance is the intrinsic fracture energy Γ0 = τcδc (Hui and Long 2026, Eq. 10).

A material point passes through the zone in a time of about lc/v. Compare it with the creep time tc of topic 16.

  • Slow crack, lc/v much longer than tc. The material relaxes as it is loaded, so the whole body is elastic with G∞. Almost nothing is dissipated, and the crack needs only Γ0.
  • Fast crack, lc/v much shorter than tc. Near the zone the material has no time to creep and responds with G0; far away it has relaxed. The zone slides as in a stiff solid, so under the same remote load it opens less. The energy released far away must be larger to break it.

Under small-scale damage, a zone much smaller than the body, these are the classical limits of Knauss (1973), Schapery (1975), de Gennes (1996) and Persson and Brener (2005) for the energy Γ that drives the crack at a steady speed v, which in steady growth is also the energy it needs (Hui and Long 2026, Eq. 55):

Plotted against the logarithm of the speed, Γ rises between the limits along an S-shaped curve (Hui and Long 2026, p. 3). The difference Γ − Γ0 is dissipated in the bulk (their Eq. 11):

ΓD is the energy dissipated in the bulk per unit crack advance. At high speed Γ = Γ0/λ, so the bulk takes the fraction 1 − λ: almost all of it when λ is small.

Why G0/G∞? Let KIII be the mode III stress intensity factor seen from far outside the zone (topic 1). The material there has relaxed, so it sends energy KIII²/(2G∞) per unit advance towards the tip, the J integral of topic 11. In an elastic solid of shear modulus μ, a strip zone breaks when KIII²/(2μ) reaches Γ0. A slow zone slides as in a solid with G∞, a fast zone as in one with G0:

So the fast crack needs a KIII larger by √(G0/G∞), and releases G0/G∞ times more energy. This argument is consistent with Eqs. 53 to 55 of Hui and Long (2026). Under small-scale damage the zone also grows with speed: lc/lc0 = Γ/Γ0 (their Eq. 56).

Watch out. The limit G0/G∞ assumes that the body can supply that much energy. In a thin strip the stress far ahead cannot exceed τc, so the stored energy caps Γ, and the curve can stop at a terminal speed below the limit. That case is the subject of the viscoelastic crack study. The effect can be large: Hui and Long (2026, p. 13) take λ of about 10−3 for highly viscoelastic solids, and use G0/G∞ = 800 in an example (p. 9).

Try it. A solid has G0/G∞ = 50 and intrinsic fracture energy Γ0 = 50 J/m². In a large specimen, so that damage is small-scale, what energy per unit area does a very fast crack need? Γ = J/m²

Show the working

The very fast crack needs fifty times its intrinsic fracture energy. Of the 2500 J/m², 2450 J/m², or 98 percent, is dissipated in the bulk.

Used in: the viscoelastic crack, the problem and steps 5 and 6.

18 When does a crack spread across a film?

A thin film bonded to a thicker substrate is often in tension, for example after it is deposited hot and cooled, or as a paint dries. A crack can then cut through the thickness of the film and spread across it, like the cracks in dried mud or in the glaze on a pot. This is a channel crack.

The crack starts at a flaw. Once it is longer than several film thicknesses, it is close to steady state: the conditions at its advancing edge no longer depend on its length (shown in three dimensions by Nakamura and Kamath 1992, for a film on a rigid substrate; Xia and Hutchinson 2000, p. 1108). The energy released per unit area of new crack is then a constant.

That constant follows from two-dimensional problems. When the edge advances by a unit length, a unit length of uncracked section far ahead is in effect replaced by a unit length of cracked section far behind. The region around the edge is carried along unchanged, so the energy released is the difference between the elastic energies of these two cross-sections of film and substrate, each a plane-strain problem (topic 2). For a crack that reaches the substrate, Beuth (1992) found the energy release rate, averaged over the advancing edge (Xia and Hutchinson 2000, Eq. 1):

Here h is the film thickness and σ0 is the uniform stress in the film before cracking, acting across the crack line. E is the plane-strain modulus of the film, the E′ of topic 2, with E and ν its Young’s modulus and Poisson’s ratio. The dimensionless function g depends on the Dundurs parameters α and β, two numbers that measure the elastic mismatch between film and substrate. g grows large for a stiff film on a compliant substrate (their Fig. 1).

Let Gc be the mode I toughness of the film, the Γ of topic 4. Cracks channel across the film when G reaches Gc (their Eq. 3). Short cracks and flaws release less than the steady value, so this condition is a safe basis for design against extensive film cracking (p. 1109).

Xia and Hutchinson also use a simpler model (their Section 2). The film is a membrane in plane stress. The substrate is a bed of springs that pulls the film back with a force k per unit area per unit displacement. Take x1 along the crack and x2 across it, in the plane of the film. Far behind the edge of an isolated crack, the stress across the crack recovers with distance from it (from their Eq. 9):

The changes caused by the crack decay over the length ℓ (their Eq. 12). It is not the material length of topic 9.

In this model the energy release rate is the first form below (their Eq. 10). Choosing k to match Beuth’s result ties ℓ to the film thickness (their Eqs. 11 and 12):

Without mismatch (α = β = 0), ℓ = 1.98h (p. 1113), so g = 1.26.

Watch out. G is the energy per unit area of new crack: the energy released when the edge advances by a unit length, divided by the film thickness h. And the crack faces are free of total traction: the prestress σ0 plus the change caused by the crack is zero there, not the change alone.

Try it. A film with no elastic mismatch has h = 1 µm, E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.2 and σ0 = 200 MPa. These inputs are hypothetical, like the others on this page. Find the energy release rate of a steady channel crack. G = J/m²

Show the working

Without mismatch, (π/2)g = ℓ/h = 1.98. Use Pa and m:

The film releases 1.086 J for each square metre of new crack. The model form gives the same: G = σ0²ℓ/E with ℓ = 1.98 µm. At the same stress, a film twice as thick would release twice as much. The crack channels if the film’s toughness Gc is no more than this.

Used in: thin-film cracking, the problem and steps 1, 4 and 5.

19 How can atoms flowing into a grain boundary open a crack?

A polycrystalline metal film is made of many small crystals, called grains, which meet at grain boundaries; in thin films many grains run through the whole thickness. At high temperature atoms move along the boundaries and along the free surface. A boundary under tension attracts atoms: plating them onto it inserts extra material between the two grains, which relaxes the tension across it. Films of copper, silver, platinum and gold without an adherent surface oxide lose almost all their stress above the temperatures at which grain-boundary diffusion can occur (Gao, Zhang, Nix, Thompson and Arzt 1999, Section 1).

Gao and coworkers took one boundary, from the surface at depth z = 0 to the substrate at z = h, the film thickness. The film cannot slide on the substrate, no atoms move along the interface, and fast surface diffusion keeps the surface flat (their Sections 1 and 2.1).

What drives the atoms is their chemical potential μ, the change in energy when one atom is added. Inserting an atom of volume Ω into a boundary under a normal traction σgb lets the traction do work σgbΩ, so relative to a flat free surface (their Eq. 3):

Atoms flow from high to low μ: from the surface into a boundary in tension. Under compression they flow out of it (their Section 4).

Along the boundary the flux runs down the gradient of μ, towards higher traction: per unit length out of the plane it is δgbDgb/(kT) times ∂σgb/∂z (their Eq. 4). Here δgb is the thickness of the boundary, Dgb the diffusivity of atoms in it, k Boltzmann’s constant and T the absolute temperature. Arriving atoms plate onto the boundary, so its opening 2u grows where the flux converges (their Eqs. 5 and 6). 2u is the full gap, the δ of Conventions; δgb is a thickness, not a gap.

The plated material is a wedge. A layer of thickness b inserted from the surface down to a depth z is, elastically, an edge dislocation with Burgers vector b at z, so the wedge is a continuous array of climb-edge dislocations (their Section 2.1). Its elastic field compresses the boundary, lowering the traction (their Eq. 2). The traction is zero at the surface, and at the interface, with no sliding and no diffusion, the wedge stays closed (their Eqs. 8 and 9).

The traction then decays as a sum of modes, each falling as e−λnt/t0 with a pure number λn (their Eq. 11). The unit of time is (their Eq. 12):

E* is the plane-strain modulus, the E′ of topic 2. The unit grows as the cube of the film thickness, one power of h from each of three steps:

Here ∼ means “of the order of”. The stiffness of the wedge per unit opening is of order E*/h, so cancelling the initial traction σ0 needs an opening of about σ0h/E*; the traction gradient that drives the atoms is of order σ0/h, and the flux converges over a path of length h. The stress cancels; the 4π in t0 comes from the dislocation solution.

Every mode decays, so at long times the boundary is free of traction while the wedge holds it open. The film far away still carries σ0: the wedge relaxes the boundary, not the whole film (their Section 4). Film and substrate have the same elastic constants in the paper, so the boundary is a traction-free edge crack of depth h in a half-space, with its tip at the interface. Only the traction σ0 removed from its faces matters for K (topic 5), so K is that of an edge crack under remote tension σ0. The paper finds it approaching this value on a time scale of order t0/λ1 (p. 2870 and their Fig. 7):

This is the formula of topic 3 with a = h and the handbook edge-crack factor Y = 1.1215. The crack forms without creating any new free surface (p. 2867), and its singular stress at the interface may nucleate dislocations (their Section 4).

Watch out. t0 sets the unit of time; it is not the relaxation time itself. The slowest mode decays at the rate λ1 = 11.74 in units of 1/t0 (their Table 1), so its e-folding time is t0/λ1 ≈ 0.085t0, about twelve times shorter. The difference mattered in the grain-boundary wedge study.

Try it. In a film 0.5 µm thick, the traction on an isolated grain boundary decays with an e-folding time of 10 minutes. What is the e-folding time in a film of the same material 1 µm thick, at the same temperature? These inputs are hypothetical, like the others on this page. time = min

Show the working

The e-folding time is te = t0/λ1. For the same material at the same temperature, everything in t0 except h is unchanged, and λ1 = 11.74 for an isolated boundary. With h1 = 0.5 µm and h2 = 1 µm:

Doubling the thickness makes the relaxation eight times slower, not two or four times. For the thinner film the unit is t0 = 11.74 × 10 min ≈ 117 min. The answer needs the same λ1 in both films. For boundaries spaced two film thicknesses apart, λ1 is about twice the isolated value (their Section 3.2), and it changes with the ratio of thickness to spacing (their Eq. B9).

Used in: the grain-boundary wedge, steps 1, 2, 4 and 5.
